title: North Korea fires short-range missiles in second launch within a week
excerpt: South Korea says Pyongyang launched from Wonsan toward the East Sea; Seoul convened an emergency security meeting and urged an immediate halt, calling the tests a grave UN resolution violation.
body:
• North Korea fired short-range ballistic missiles toward the East Sea on Sunday from the Wonsan area, the second launch in about a week, according to South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff and Japan's defence ministry.
  • The first missile flew roughly 450 kilometres and fell outside Japan's exclusive economic zone; Pyongyang later fired additional unidentified projectiles.
  • It was North Korea's 14th ballistic missile launch this year and came days after Pyongyang dismissed a UN nuclear watchdog resolution against its nuclear programme.
  • South Korea convened an emergency National Security Council meeting and urged an immediate halt, calling the launches a grave violation of UN Security Council resolutions.

North Korea launched short-range ballistic missiles toward the East Sea on Sunday, in its second missile test in about a week and its 14th ballistic launch of the year, according to South Korean and Japanese officials.

South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said Pyongyang fired the missiles from the Wonsan area in the afternoon. The first flew about 450 kilometres over the East Sea before landing in the water; Japan's defence ministry said it appeared to have fallen outside Japan's exclusive economic zone. North Korea later fired additional unidentified projectiles, which South Korea said were still being analysed for type, range and altitude.

The launch was the first since September 12, when the North fired several ballistic missiles a day after the conclusion of Freedom Edge — a multidomain exercise involving South Korea, the United States and Japan.

Seoul and Tokyo respond

South Korea's National Security Office convened an emergency security meeting with the defence ministry and the Joint Chiefs of Staff on Sunday, and said it had "analysed and assessed the impact of this launch on our security and reviewed the measures required."

"South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said Pyongyang fired the missiles from the Wonsan area in the afternoon."

"North Korea's ballistic missile launch is a grave act that violates United Nations Security Council resolutions," the office said in a statement, urging an "immediate halt." South Korea's military added that it was closely monitoring the North "under the staunch South Korea-US combined defence posture."

Japan's defence minister Shinjiro Koizumi strongly condemned the launch, Kyodo News reported.

Context & Background

The test fits an escalating pattern of defiance. A day before the launch, North Korea dismissed a resolution by the UN nuclear watchdog against its nuclear programme in a statement carried by state media. Last week, Pyongyang condemned a US-led naval drill — which included South Korea and Japan and ran from August 29 to September 10 near Guam — as a "frantic military move" meant to preserve US hegemony in the Asia-Pacific.

On Friday, Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un, blamed US-led military drills for "ever-worsening" tensions on the Korean Peninsula and vowed no change in the country's drive to strengthen its nuclear arsenal — shrugging off recent US gestures, including a scaling back of a joint military exercise with South Korea, aimed at reviving diplomacy.

Impact & Analysis

The back-to-back launches — September 12 and September 20 — suggest Pyongyang is settling into a rapid testing cadence timed to allied military activity. Each cycle follows the same script: a US-allied drill concludes, the North responds with launches, and Kim Yo Jong delivers the rhetorical follow-up. The difference this time is the explicit rejection of diplomatic off-ramps, with the IAEA resolution dismissal signalling that Pyongyang intends to normalise both its nuclear and missile programmes regardless of international pressure.

For the region, the practical risk is a misread launch during a busy exercise calendar — South Korea and Japan remain on a hair-trigger for extended-range tests that could overfly the archipelago.

Diaspora Angle

Regional instability on the Korean Peninsula matters for the large Indian diaspora across East and Southeast Asia and for global markets, where another escalation cycle would feed energy prices and supply-chain risk.

What's Next

Attention now turns to whether Pyongyang follows the two launches with a longer-range test or a satellite launch — its customary escalation steps. Seoul and Washington will weigh whether to adjust the autumn exercise schedule, the variable that has triggered most of this year's launches.
